An example: a kernel that boots in QEMU

text: Vibe is suited to drivers and kernels: device registers are described with structs, privileged instructions are called like ordinary functions, and the program is built without libc. Everything you need is built into the language and the prelude. No macros, no #pragma , no compiler attributes. Task In C In Vibe a device register volatile uint32_t * and macros volatile u32* reg or volatile u32 in a struct a descriptor format __attribute__((packed)) packed struct I/O ports asm volatile with constraints Port::in8(p) , Port::out8(p, v) cli , hlt , rdtsc , cr3 , MSRs your own inline asm for each Cpu::cli() , Cpu::halt() , Cpu::rdtsc() , Cpu::cr3() , Cpu::rdmsr(n) register bits masks and shifts by hand Bits::get(v, 7, 4) , Bits::set(v, 7, 4, x) atomic operations, a spinlock stdatomic.h Atomic::cas32(...) , Spinlock no libc -nostdlib -ffreestanding and scripts --freestanding # volatile volatile goes before the type and means that every read and write goes to memory: the compiler does not merge or drop them. This is needed for device registers. Output volatile applies to what lies at the address: volatile u32* p is a pointer to a volatile u32 . A field volatile u32 data and a variable volatile u32 x work too. The width of an access always equals the width of the type: volatile u8* reads exactly one byte, volatile u16* two. Output The real address of registers is given as a number through as : auto uart = 0xFE201000 as *Uart; . # packed struct An ordinary struct aligns its fields as in C. A packed struct puts the fields back to back, without gaps: this is how descriptors, IDT and GDT tables, packet headers and PCI configuration are laid out. Output Access to unaligned fields is ordinary: x86-64 allows it. Aligning a struct type by hand is not supported yet (see align(N) for global variables below): align the buffers you need in the linker script. # Register bits: Bits Output Function What it does Bits::bit(n) a number with the single bit n Bits::mask(hi, lo) a mask of the bits hi..lo inclusive Bits::get(v, hi, lo) the value of a bit field Bits::set(v, hi, lo, x) v with the field replaced The results have the type u64 ; for a 32-bit register add as u32 : narrowing in Vibe is always explicit. # The processor: Cpu , and ports: Port These are ordinary static methods. Privileged instructions crash in an ordinary program, so use them in a kernel or a driver. Function Instruction Cpu::cli() , Cpu::sti() disable and enable interrupts Cpu::halt() , Cpu::pause() , Cpu::nop() , Cpu::breakpoint() hlt , pause , nop , int3 Cpu::fence() , load_fence() , store_fence() mfence , lfence , sfence Cpu::rdtsc() the cycle counter Cpu::cr0() , cr2() , cr3() , cr4() and set_cr0(v) , set_cr3(v) , set_cr4(v) control registers Cpu::load_idt(p) , load_gdt(p) , invlpg(addr) lidt , lgdt , invlpg Cpu::rdmsr(n) , Cpu::wrmsr(n, v) model-specific registers Port::in8(p) , in16 , in32 in Port::out8(p, v) , out16 , out32 out rdtsc , pause and the barriers also work in ordinary programs: Output # align(N) : aligning a global variable Page tables and DMA buffers must lie at an address that is a multiple of the page size. Write align(N) before a global variable; N is a power of two. Output A struct type can be aligned too: align(64) struct Line { u8 tag; i64 val; } makes alignof(Line) and sizeof(Line) 64, and every variable, array element and field of that type is placed accordingly. The own backend handles locals aligned to 16; for more the compiler switches to LLVM by itself. # Atomic operations and Spinlock Output Function What it does Atomic::fetch_add32(p, v) , fetch_add8 , fetch_add16 , fetch_add64 adds and returns the old value Atomic::swap32(p, v) , swap8 , swap16 , swap64 writes and returns the old value Atomic::cas32(p, expected, desired) , cas8 , cas16 , cas64 writes desired if expected is there; returns the previous value # asm : your own instructions If the instruction you need is not in Cpu , you can insert it yourself: asm Type ( template , constraints , operands...) . The template and the constraints are in the LLVM (AT T) syntax. Curly braces in the strings are escaped: \{rax\} . The own backend encodes only the templates that the prelude uses (they are listed above). title: Testing

headings.text: Running from an editor and in CI

text: Tests are built into the language: a special test block is written next to the code, and the command vibe test runs them. No separate libraries or configuration files are needed. # The first test Test output Run it with the command: test name { ... } is a top-level declaration. Inside is ordinary code. A test is a function that returns !void , so ? works in it. A test passes if the block reaches its end. It fails if an assert or panic fires, or if ? receives an error. # What vibe test does Compiles the file with all the test blocks (and with all its imports). Runs each test in a separate process . The failure of one (even a crash) does not break the others. Prints ok or FAIL for each and a summary. For failed tests, shows everything they printed. Returns exit code 0 if nothing failed, and 1 if something did. test blocks are ignored by vibe run and vibe build . A file with tests remains an ordinary program. # What failures look like Test output Each failure shows its reason: error: Name : ? propagated an error; assertion failed (file:line) : the condition in assert is false; panic: message (file:line) : panic was called. The output of passed tests is hidden: it is needed only when something is broken. # assert assert(condition) checks a bool . If the condition is false, the program ends with a message and a location. It works not only in tests but in ordinary code too: Output exit code 1 assert has no separate message. If you need context, use panic with a format: Output exit code 1 # Testing errors An expected error is checked with catch : Test output The pattern is this: catch |e| checks the error and leaves the test through return . If there was no error, control reaches assert(false) and the test fails. # Testing with memory Tests can allocate memory like ordinary code. Create an allocator inside the test and free through defer : Test output The last test shows the advantage of explicit allocators: the behavior when memory runs out is checked deterministically, with no hacks. # Organization Tests are usually written in the same file , under the code they check: then nothing needs to be imported. If there are many tests, create a separate file and import the module: mathx.vibe Test output Only the tests of the file you specified are run. The test blocks of imported files are not run. Test names may repeat (the compiler does not check), but it is better if they are unique: you find the failed test by its name. # A file without tests If a file has no test blocks at all, the command reports 0 passed, 0 failed and exits with code 0. Do not confuse this with all tests passed . # Running from an editor and in CI In VS Code / code-oss the extension shows a run button above every test (see tooling ). In CI one command is enough: vibe test main.vibe . Exit code 1 means a failure. The optimization mode can be switched: vibe test main.vibe -O runs the same tests through LLVM -O2 . Useful for making sure optimizations do not change the behavior. # What next Failing tests often come down to errors: errors and optional values . How the compiler's own test suite is organized: how it all works .

title: Tools: fmt, lsp, flags
text: All the tools are subcommands of one executable, vibe . Nothing separate needs to be installed. # Compiler diagnostics Every error is printed in the form file:line: error: message , and under it the source line is shown with a ^ pointing at the place of the error: Compiler output When the program has a similar name, the compiler suggests it (for names shorter than three characters no suggestions are shown, they would be random): an unknown variable or function; a struct field, an enum or union variant, a name in a closure's capture list; the name of a generic constraint ( T: Orb → Ord ). Typical messages and their causes are explained on the page pitfalls and FAQ . Note: the compiler stops at the first parser error. It also reports type errors one per run, but the language server checks every function separately and shows one error per function. # vibe fmt vibe fmt file.vibe ... rewrites files in place. The formatter works on tokens: it fixes spaces, indentation and blank lines, never wraps or joins lines and does not touch comments. What exactly the formatter does: indentation is 4 spaces per level of bracket nesting; a continuation of an expression on the next line gets one more level; spaces around binary operators, after commas and colons, inside { } on one line; no spaces inside () and [] ; the angle brackets of generics ( List i64 ) stay as written; runs of blank lines collapse into one, and blank lines right after { and before } are removed; trailing spaces are removed, and the file ends with exactly one newline; the distance between code and a trailing comment is kept as it is. What the formatter does not do: it does not break long lines, does not align comments to a column, does not reorder declarations, does not rename anything. Spaces around * and , when the neighboring tokens do not show whether it is multiplication or a pointer ( i*2 in the example above), are left as they were. --check changes nothing and prints would reformat file for every file that would be changed, and exits with code 1: handy for CI: The formatter is idempotent: running it again on an already formatted file changes nothing. It is guaranteed to preserve the stream of tokens: the meaning of the program cannot change. Note: files with \r\n line endings are turned into \n by the formatter. # Compilation modes Vibe has two backends: the own x86-64 backend (the default). The compiler itself turns the intermediate representation into machine code and writes an ELF object. The build is very fast; the code is noticeably faster than naive code because there is register allocation, but slower than optimized LLVM; LLVM ( --llvm , -O , --release ): the compiler prints LLVM IR, and clang optimizes and compiles it. Command Backend Optimization Bounds checks vibe run x.vibe own none yes vibe run x.vibe --llvm LLVM -O0 yes vibe run x.vibe -O LLVM -O2 yes vibe run x.vibe --release LLVM -O2 no vibe run x.vibe --no-safety own none no The bounds check is what turns going out of an array into a clear panic. Without it this is undefined behavior : the example below fails with a panic in a normal build and silently reads garbage with --release : ( oob.vibe reads a[5] of an array of three elements.) Keep debug builds with the checks, and turn on --release for finished programs when you are sure the indexes are correct. For development use the default mode: it builds the compiler itself (about 12 thousand lines of Vibe) in about a tenth of a second, not counting the link. # Intermediate representations vibe ir file.vibe prints the LLVM IR that the frontend generated. It is the same text that the own backend reads. For the function you get (local variables live in alloca , the names %tN are temporary values): vibe tokens file.vibe prints the tokens: the line number, the kind of the token and the text. Useful when it is unclear how the lexer split a line (especially with quotes and curly braces): How everything else works is on the page how the compiler works . # Language server and editor vibe lsp is a language server over the LSP protocol on standard input/output. It is built on the same parser and generator as the compiler, so the messages are the same as with vibe build , and they also apply to unsaved changes. Features: Feature What it can do Diagnostics errors with an exact range as you type, did you mean hints, quick fixes Hover the signature of a symbol and the /// comments above the declaration Completion struct members and methods (by the inferred type) after . , - and :: , module names after alias:: , enum variants after . , literal fields after . inside Name{ ... } , local variables, global names, keywords Parameter hints when typing ( and , : the signature of the function or method being called Go to definition including into imported files and by the path inside import ... title: Projects and dependencies
text: A single file is enough to start. When a program grows into several files, C code or other people's libraries, describe it in a vibe.toml and vibe run , vibe build and vibe test work without a file name. The commands find vibe.toml in the current directory or any directory above it, so they also work from src/sub/ . A file named on the command line ( vibe run tools/gen.vibe ) inside a project still gets the project's dependencies, C sources and libraries. # vibe.toml The format is a small part of TOML: sections, key = value , strings, integers, booleans, lists and inline tables, and # comments. A mistake is reported with the line: vibe.toml:2: error: unterminated string . # Dependencies A dependency is imported by its name: path dependencies point to a directory on disk. git dependencies are cloned into .vibe/deps/NAME the first time a command needs them ( rev is a tag or branch). Delete the directory to fetch again. A dependency with its own vibe.toml brings its own dependencies, C sources and libraries along. Without a manifest, its lib file is src/lib.vibe or lib.vibe . Imports that start with ./ or ../ are always relative files, so a dependency name never hides them. The language server reads the same manifest, so imports of dependencies are found in the editor too.

text: Besides the prelude, which every program gets automatically, the standard library has modules that you import by name. They are built into the compiler, so there is nothing to install: Always give a module a name with as : its functions are then written fs::list_dir(...) and do not mix with your own names. Module What is in it std/fs file metadata, directories, walking a tree, copying, moving, removing, temporary directories std/path path strings: join , base , dir , ext , stem , normalize , relative , absolute std/time wall clock, DateTime with time zones, parsing and printing ISO 8601, Stopwatch , sleep_ms std/os running programs and capturing their output, environment variables, cpu_count , exe_path std/args command-line options with --help std/json JSON parsing with error positions, a tree you can query and build, and a streaming Builder std/net TCP sockets and DNS (see networking and threads ) std/http an HTTP/1.1 client and a small server std/thread threads, Mutex , Cond , WaitGroup , Channel T Like everything in Vibe, nothing here allocates on its own: functions that return new strings or lists take an Allocator , and the results have a deinit() or are freed with that allocator. # std/fs Output Function What it does info(p) , link_info(p) Info{ kind, size, modified, mode } ; kind is .File , .Dir , .Link or .Other exists , is_dir , is_file list_dir(a, p) a DirList sorted by name: for (auto e : d.slice()) { e.name; e.kind } walk(a, root) , walk_all(a, root) every file below root (with directories for walk_all ), as relative paths make_dir , make_dirs one directory, or with every missing parent remove_file , remove_dir , remove_all(a, p) move(from, to) , copy_file(from, to) , append_file(p, data) , set_mode(p, mode) cwd(a) , set_cwd(p) , temp_dir(a, prefix) Errors are the usual names: error.NotFound , error.PermissionDenied , error.AlreadyExists , error.DirectoryNotEmpty , error.NotADirectory . title: Networking and threads
text: # std/thread Output spawn runs a closure on a new thread. The closure keeps pointers to what it captures, so join every thread before those variables go out of scope . spawn_fn(f, arg) starts a plain fn(void*) instead. Type What it is Thread join() , detach() Mutex lock() , unlock() , try_lock() ; the zero value is ready Cond wait( m) , wait_ms( m, ms) , signal() , broadcast() AtomicI64 add(d) (returns the old value), load() , store(x) , compare_swap(old, new) WaitGroup add(n) , done() , wait() Channel T a bounded queue: Channel T ::create(a, capacity) , send(v) , recv() , try_recv() , close() , destroy() parallel_for(n, threads, body) calls body(i) for every i in 0..n , split over threads threads (0 means one per CPU), and returns when all are done. Locks, channels and wait groups must not be copied once used: share them through a pointer (a channel is created on the heap for that reason). Output # std/net Output listen(host, port) gives a Listener with accept() , port() and close() (which also wakes up a thread blocked in accept ). connect_to(host, port) gives a Conn : read(buf) (0 at the end), write_all(s) , print(...) with interpolation and no allocation, set_timeout(ms) , close_write() , close() , peer(buf) . Reader::init( conn, buf) buffers reads: read_line() , read_exact( list, n) , read_all( list) . Errors: error.HostNotFound , error.ConnectionRefused , error.AddressInUse , error.TimedOut , error.ConnectionReset . # std/http The client speaks HTTP/1.1 over http:// and https:// . HTTPS uses the system's OpenSSL library ( libssl.so.3 ), loaded the first time it is needed, so programs need no extra link flags; certificates and host names are checked against the system store. Request fields: method ( GET ), url , headers , body , timeout_ms (30000), max_redirects (5), insecure (skip certificate checks), ca_file (trust these PEM certificates instead of the system store). Reply : status , reason , headers , body , header(name) (case-insensitive), ok() , deinit() . Chunked bodies and redirects are handled. Errors: error.UnsupportedScheme , error.InvalidUrl , error.CertificateInvalid , error.TlsUnavailable (no libssl), plus the network errors above. url_encode(a, s) , url_decode(a, s) , parse_url(s) . The server runs a handler on a pool of threads, keeps connections alive and gives every request its own arena: Output ServerRequest : method , path , query , headers , body , peer , header(name) , param(name) (decoded query parameter), and a , an allocator freed after the handler returns. ServerResponse : set status (200), header(name, value) , then exactly one of text , html , json , send(content_type, body) or printf(content_type, ...) . serve(a, threads, handler) blocks until stop() . The handler runs on several threads at once: guard shared data with a Mutex or use atomics. The server speaks plain HTTP; put it behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) for HTTPS.

text: This page collects what is not obvious: places where you can make a mistake and places where Vibe works differently from the languages you are used to. Every pitfall has an example. If you got a strange result or an error, look here. # Numbers # A literal must fit its type Compiler output const u8 b = 300; and const u32 x = -1; are compile errors. A value computed at run time still wraps silently (see below). # Integers overflow without a warning Output The result wraps around within the type. To catch it, build with --check-overflow (a panic with file and line) or compute in a wider type. # Integer division by zero panics Output exit code 1 It is a panic, not an error : it cannot be caught with catch , and the message has the file and line. Check the divisor before dividing. In --release the check is removed. # / on integers drops the fraction 7 / 2 is 3 , and -7 / 2 is -3 (towards zero). For a fractional result convert: 7 as f64 / 2 as f64 . # Floating-point literals hide imprecision 0.1 + 0.2 is printed as 0.3 because the output goes through %g . But 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false . Compare floats with a tolerance. # Narrowing and a change of sign only through as const i32 small = big; will not compile. This is deliberate: Conversions are visible . # 300 as u8 from a literal A literal in as is handled as a constant and may not be truncated. To check the behavior, put the number in a variable: auto n = 300; n as u8 gives 44. # Strings # { in a string opens an interpolation Output The compiler took { key ... for an interpolation of the string key , and instead of JSON you got an unexpected output. Write a literal brace as {{ and }} : Output # Interpolation works only in print functions const auto s = n = {n} ; is an error. Build a string value with bprint or sprint (see strings ). # You cannot modify a literal Output exit code 1 Writing into a literal crashes the program. Copy into a buffer. # str is bytes, not characters привет .len is 12 , not 6 . Indexing gives bytes. For ASCII everything is simple; for other scripts you have to parse UTF-8 by hand. # A slice of a string does not end with a zero byte puts(s[0..2].ptr) will print the whole original string. For C use to_cstr or dupz (see C ). # There is no + for strings Joining is done with str_join , str_concat , bprint or sprint ; there are also str_split , str_replace and str_to_upper (see the reference ). They take an Allocator because the result is a new string. # A wrong format is printed as bad format The specification is checked when printing, not at compile time. An unknown letter ( {n:b} ) or a format that does not suit the type gives bad format in the output, and the program goes on. # There is no binary output The format {n:b} is not supported: the allowed ones for integers are d , i , u , x , X , o , c . # Variables and scopes # A parameter is a copy Output Parameters and variables are mutable, but the function changes its own copy. To forbid changing a parameter, write const i64 x . To change the caller's data, pass a pointer. # The same name twice in one block Compiler output In a nested block you can shadow, in the same one you cannot. # A variable hides a function const auto max = 5; makes the call max(1, 2) impossible in that block. # The names from the prelude are taken You cannot declare functions max , min , abs , sort , swap , run , env , arg , cstr : duplicate function . Choose other names. # A global array requires an initializer i64[3] arr; at the top level without = ... does not compile. Write i64[3] arr = [0, 0, 0]; . # A const with a function call is evaluated every time const auto K = next(); at the top level is a substitution of the expression, and the side effect fires at every use. # Control flow # A forgotten ; Every statement ends with ; . Without it the compiler stops at the next token: Compiler output # if is not an expression auto x = if (a) { 1 } else { 2 }; is an error. Use match ( match a { true = 1, false = 2 } ) or a variable declared in advance. # In a catch block an expression must come last A block that ends with a match or if as a statement does not count as a value. Put the result in a variable and make it the last line. # The condition must be bool if (n) and while (p) do not work. Write n != 0 and p != null . # No 0..=n , a, b = b, a , x++ as an expression This is deliberate: one form per action. x++ and the compound assignments ( += -= *= /= %= |= = ^= = = ) exist, but only as statements. # break and continue name a loop through a label To leave an outer loop, label it ( outer: for (...) ) and write break outer; . Without a label they affect the nearest loop. # A match statement does not have to be complete A forgotten variant causes no error: nothing simply happens. For a match expression, exhaustiveness is checked. # A function must return a value on every path Compiler output The compiler checks that a function with a result never falls off its end. A path returns when it ends in return , an if with an else where both branches return, a match where every arm returns, an endless while (true) without a break , or a call to panic . # Errors and optional values # catch and orelse take everything to the right f(5) catch 0 + 100 is f(5) catch (0 + 100) , the result is 5 , not 105 . Use parentheses: (f(5) catch 0) + 100 . # ? only in a function with !T In an ordinary function ? is not allowed: there is nowhere to propagate to. # You cannot ignore a !T f() without ? , catch or _ = does not compile. # ?T is not compared with null For ?T use orelse , is .None , match . Only ordinary pointers can be compared with null . # catch return) in parentheses In a call argument, catch return before the closing parenthesis is not parsed. Put the result in a variable on a separate line. # Types and structs # A struct literal only with a capital letter point{ .x = 1 } is not recognized: T{ is taken as a literal when the type name starts with a capital letter. # Missing fields are zeros P{ .x = 1 } zeroes t

title: How it all works
text: This page is for those who want to understand what happens under the hood, or who are going to change the compiler. It is not required for writing programs. # The pipeline The compiler is a program in Vibe itself, about 12 thousand lines in the selfhost/ directory. It works as a pipeline: What each file does: File Role lexer.vibe tokens (see lexical structure ) ast.vibe fat tree nodes with a kind tag parser.vibe parsing the syntax, splitting {x} into parts gen.vibe types, instantiating generics, functions, diagnostics gen_stmt.vibe statements, defer / errdefer , match gen_expr.vibe expressions, addresses, operators, casts gen_call.vibe calls, inferring type parameters, methods, function pointers gen_fmt.vibe building Fmt for calls with interpolation, panic , assert , embed resolve.vibe , loader.vibe imports and module prefixes native.vibe the own backend: IR → x86-64 (System V ABI), register allocation x64.vibe the instruction encoder and the ELF64 object writer fmt.vibe the vibe fmt formatter lsp.vibe , ide.vibe , analysis.vibe , json.vibe , textpos.vibe the language server diag.vibe nice error messages, did you mean main.vibe the command-line driver You can see the intermediate results right from the CLI: vibe tokens file.vibe (tokens) and vibe ir file.vibe (LLVM IR). More in tooling . The prelude ( std/std.vibe ) is built into the compiler through embed , so vibe is one executable without external data. # Two backends The own one (default). It parses the textual LLVM IR that the frontend generated and turns it into x86-64 machine code. It uses linear-scan register allocation, fusing a comparison with a branch, constants in operands, and lazy loading of composite values. There is not a single line of LLVM inside. The purpose is a fast build: a typical project builds in fractions of a second. LLVM ( -O , --release , --llvm ). The same IR is handed to clang , which does full optimization. It is needed for speed in production builds. A comparison for a program of 10 thousand lines, from source to executable (the author's measurements): Builder Time vibe, own backend about 95 ms clang -O0 about 220 ms gcc -O0 about 670 ms And the speed of the result (recursive fib(38) and a sieve of 50 million): fib(38) sieve 50M C ( clang -O2 ) 97 ms 369 ms Vibe --release 95 ms 345 ms Vibe, own backend about 290 ms about 820 ms So --release does not lose to C, and the debug build wins in compile speed. # Self-hosting and the fixed point The compiler builds itself. To start from zero, the repository holds a seed : the LLVM IR of the compiler itself ( bootstrap/seed.ll.gz ). clang turns it into the first working compiler. The check: stage2 and stage3 are identical byte for byte (the fixed point). The same is done for the chain with the own backend without LLVM (native2 == native3). The script bootstrap.sh runs everything, then runs the test suite and puts the result into build/vibe . A consequence for development: a new language feature is added in two steps. First the compiler is taught the feature without using it in its own sources, and the seed is updated ( tools/update-seed.sh ). Only then can the feature be used in selfhost/ : otherwise the old seed cannot build the new code. # The memory layout of types The principle what you see is what is in memory : Type In memory i8..i64 , u8..u64 an integer of the corresponding size bool one byte T* a pointer, 8 bytes T[] , str { ptr, len } , 16 bytes T[N] N elements in a row struct the fields in order, alignment as in C enum a 32-bit integer union { i32 tag, payload } , the payload sized for the largest variant !T { i32 error code, T } fn(A) - R a function pointer fn[](A) - R a pair: a function pointer and a context pointer This explains why structs can be passed to C (by pointer), why nothing needs to be packed at a call and why sizeof is predictable. # How interpolation is expanded The compiler knows neither print nor println . It knows one rule: if the last parameter of the called function has the type Fmt (declared in std/std.vibe ), all the remaining arguments and strings with {...} are gathered into a Fmt value. Fmt is a list of pieces: literal text, a pointer to a value, a function that knows how to print a value of that type, and a specification ( :08X , :.2 and so on). The print functions for structs, enums, unions and arrays are generated by the compiler from the type as ordinary Vibe code. For numbers, strings and pointers the functions from the prelude are used ( __fmt_int , __fmt_str and others). Everything lies on the caller's stack, and nothing is allocated on the heap. So interpolation is allowed where there is a function with a Fmt parameter: print , println , eprint , eprintln , panic , bprint , sprint and your own. # How generics work Functions and structs with type parameters are monomorphized : for each combination of arguments the compiler creates a separate copy. So there is no run-time overhead, and the body of a generic is checked at the use . Constraints ( T: Ord ) are checked at the call, before the body is compiled, so that the message is clear. # How defer and errdefer work The compiler expands defer into code on every path out of the block: before return , break , continue and at the end of the block. For errdefer the code is added only on the paths where an error is returned. There is no run-time machinery for this. # How ? and catch work f()? turns into a check of the error code: if it is not zero, defer and errdefer run and the same !T is returned. catch is the same check, but instead of returning it takes the branch with the fallback value. # Lazy compilation Only the functions reachable from main are compiled. An extra import does not bloat the file, and errors in dead code are not visible until it is called (unless it is a generic: then the error shows up on the first use). # Build storage Intermediate files live in .vibe-cache/ next to the place where you run the compiler: .o , .ll and test binaries.
